pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: Severe, localized abdominal pain disproportionate to physical exam findings combined with urine that darkens to a port-wine color upon standing in sunlight, triggered by low carbohydrate intake and sulfa medication. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is a rare autosomal dominant metabolic defect in the heme biosynthetic pathway, specifically caused by a deficiency in porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD). When hepatic heme synthesis is upregulated—often induced by cytochrome P450-inducing drugs like sulfonamides, low-caloric/low-carbohydrate states, or stress—there is an overwhelming accumulation of toxic upstream heme precursors: delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These neurotoxic precursors cause widespread autonomic, peripheral, and central nervous system dysfunction. This results in autonomic neuropathy (tachycardia, severe hypertension), severe visceral pain without peritoneal signs, motor axonal neuropathy (ascending paralysis), hypothalamic disruption leading to SIADH (profound hyponatremia), and acute neuro-psychiatric disturbances (hallucinations, psychosis). Sunlight causes photo-oxidation of excess porphobilinogen in the urine, producing the classic port-wine color shift.
